lower_court_summary: RiseandShine, which sells canned coffee drinks under the trademark RISE, sued PepsiCo for trademark infringement over PepsiCo's MTN DEW RISE ENERGY drink. The district court granted summary judgment to PepsiCo. In a short non-precedential order, the Second Circuit affirmed, treating the strength of the RISE mark and the overall likelihood of customer confusion as questions a judge can decide as a matter of law, and finding confusion unlikely. PepsiCo won.
question_presented: Courts in every circuit consider several factors in determining whether an alleged trademark infringer's use "is likely to cause confusion" under 15 U.S.C. § 1114. Chief among those factors is the trademark's strength, that is, its level of distinctiveness. Twelve circuits consider trademark strength an issue of fact. The Second Circuit stands alone in considering it a question of law. The question presented is: Whether trademark strength is a question of fact in a likelihood-of-confusion analysis under 15 U.S.C. § 1114.

case_name: Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc.
lower_court_summary: WBI, a natural gas pipeline company, used the eminent-domain power the Natural Gas Act gives pipeline companies to take an easement across a North Dakota family's land. After the parties agreed on compensation, the district court ordered WBI to pay the family's attorney fees under North Dakota law. The Eighth Circuit vacated the fee award, holding that because the company was using the federal government's eminent-domain power, federal law sets the compensation owed, and federal law does not include attorney fees. The pipeline company won; the landowners lost.
question_presented: The Natural Gas Act authorizes private companies to condemn land in order to build certain natural gas infrastructure, but it says nothing about how to determine the amount of just compensation owed for the property taken. 15 U.S.C. § 717f. The Third, Fifth, Sixth, and Eleventh Circuits have all held that compensation awards in private condemnations under the Natural Gas Act must therefore be determined by reference to state law, which often mandates higher compensation than the floor set by the Fifth Amendment. In this case, the Eighth Circuit expressly split with its sister circuits and instead held that the Natural Gas Act permits only the constitutional minimum of compensation required by the Fifth Amendment. The question presented is: In private condemnations under the Natural Gas Act, should just compensation be determined by reference to state law?

case_name: Suncor Energy (U.S.A.) Inc. v. Commissioners of Boulder County
lower_court_summary: Boulder County and the City of Boulder sued Suncor and ExxonMobil under Colorado law (nuisance, trespass, unjust enrichment, conspiracy), seeking damages for local harms they attribute to the companies' production, promotion and sale of fossil fuels and the resulting climate change. The companies argued that federal law preempts such state-law claims. The Colorado Supreme Court held the claims are not preempted and may go forward in state court, without deciding whether they will succeed. Boulder won.
question_presented: Whether federal law precludes state-law claims seeking relief for injuries allegedly caused by the effects of interstate and international greenhouse-gas emissions on the global climate. [Added by the Court:] Whether this Court has statutory and Article III jurisdiction to hear this case.

case_name: Crowther v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia
lower_court_summary: A former art professor (Crowther) and a former basketball coach sued the University System of Georgia, alleging sex discrimination and retaliation in their employment under Title IX. The Eleventh Circuit held that Title IX does not give employees an implied right to sue for sex discrimination in employment. It reversed the trial court's refusal to dismiss Crowther's claims and affirmed judgment against the coach. The university system won.
question_presented: Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 prohibits federally funded educational institutions from discriminating "on the basis of sex." In Cannon v. University of Chicago, 441 U.S. 677 (1979), this Court held that Title IX is privately enforceable by "victims of discrimination" through an implied right of action. And in Jackson v. Birmingham Board of Education, 544 U.S. 167 (2005), this Court held that employees of federally funded educational institutions may invoke Title IX's implied private right of action to bring claims for retaliation. Following Jackson, and until the decision below, "every ... circuit[] that has considered whether a teacher may sue under Title IX" for sex discrimination in their employment "has found they may." Pet App. 124a (Rosenbaum, J., dissenting from denial of rehearing en banc ). Splitting with eight courts of appeals, the Eleventh Circuit held in the decision below that Title IX "do[es] not embrace a private right of action for employees." Pet. App. 21a. In so holding, the Eleventh Circuit joined pre- Jackson decisions from the Fifth and Seventh Circuits in an 8-3 split. The question presented is: Whether Title IX provides employees of federally funded educational institutions a private right of action to sue for sex discrimination in employment.

lower_court_summary: Gun owners and two gun-rights groups challenged Cook County, Illinois's ban on assault weapons, including AR-15-style rifles, as a violation of the Second Amendment. In a short order, the Seventh Circuit affirmed judgment for the County. It relied on its earlier decision in Bevis v. City of Naperville, which found that the banned rifles had not been shown to differ materially from military weapons that may be banned, and said the challengers had not built a record that would justify a different result. Cook County won.
question_presented: Whether the Second and Fourteenth Amendments guarantee the right to possess AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles.
qp_note: granted on this question for both 25-238 and 25-566

lower_court_summary: Gun owners and gun-rights groups asked for preliminary injunctions against Connecticut's ban on assault weapons (including AR-15-style rifles) and large-capacity magazines, arguing it violates the Second Amendment. The district court refused. The Second Circuit affirmed, concluding the challengers had not shown they were likely to succeed on their Second Amendment claims. Connecticut won. (Argued together with Viramontes v. Cook County.)
question_presented: Whether the Second and Fourteenth Amendments guarantee the right to possess AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles.

lower_court_summary: Jouppi was convicted of flying beer into an Alaska village that bans bringing in alcohol, and state law required forfeiture of the airplane he used. He argued the forfeiture was an excessive fine under the U.S. Constitution. The Alaska Supreme Court agreed the forfeiture counts as a 'fine' but held, as a matter of law, that it was not grossly out of proportion to the offense, overruling the lower appeals court's order for more fact-finding. The State won.
question_presented: The "touchstone of the constitutional inquiry under the Excessive Fines Clause" is that the amount of the fine "must bear some relationship to the gravity of the offense that it is designed to punish." United States v. Bajakajian, 524 U.S. 321,334 (1998). Below, the Alaska Supreme Court upheld the forfeiture of petitioner's $95,000 airplane because, the court reasoned, petitioner knew that one of his passenger's grocery bags contained a sixpack of Budweiser. In so holding, the court captured vividly a lower-court conflict over the standard for evaluating the gravity of a property owner's offense under the Excessive Fines Clause. Aligning with the Eleventh Circuit, the Alaska Supreme Court examined the gravity of the defendant's offense at a stratospheric level of abstraction. Meanwhile, the federal circuit in which Alaska sits-in line with many other state and federal courts-holds that "[i]t is critical" to "review the specific actions of the violator rather than by taking an abstract view of the violation." The question presented is whether, in determining whether a fine contravenes the Excessive Fines Clause, courts may consider the gravity of the underlying offense purely in the abstract or should consider the gravity of the specific defendant's wrongdoing.

case_name: Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney's Office
lower_court_summary: Younge, the third-ranking official in the Fulton County (Georgia) District Attorney's Office, sued the office under Title VII after she was fired. Title VII does not cover the 'personal staff' of elected officials, but the office did not raise that defense until summary judgment, after discovery had closed. In an unpublished opinion, the Eleventh Circuit held the trial court could allow the late defense because it did not unfairly harm Younge, and agreed she was personal staff. The DA's office won.
question_presented: Rule 8(c)(1) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure provides that a party "must" plead "any" affirmative defense. The question presented is: Where a defendant has filed an answer without pleading an affirmative defense, may the defendant nonetheless assert that affirmative defense as the basis for a summary judgment motion, without amending or seeking to amend its answer to plead that affirmative defense, and may a defendant do so even if an amendment adding that affirmative defense would be barred by Rule 16(b)(4)?

lower_court_summary: Watanabe, held at a federal detention center in Honolulu, sued prison medical staff for money damages (a 'Bivens' claim), alleging that after an assault fractured his tailbone they gave him only over-the-counter pain medicine. The district court dismissed. The Ninth Circuit reversed, holding the claim matches Carlson v. Green, a Supreme Court case allowing such suits over inadequate prison medical care, so it is not a 'new context' that later cases bar. One judge dissented in part. The prisoner won.
question_presented: This case concerns the judicially created damages remedy first recognized in Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, 403 U.S. 388 (1971). In Carlson v. Green, 446 U.S. 14 (1980), the Court extended Bivens to an Eighth Amendment claim of deliberate indifference to medical needs where prison officials failed to address an inmate's acute asthma attack and exacerbated it, causing his death on-site within hours. Since then, this Court has emphasized that the creation of damages actions rests with Congress, not courts. The judicially created Bivens remedy thus cannot be ex-tended to any "new Bivens context" if any "special factor counsel[s] hesitation" in doing so. Ziglar v. Abbasi, 582 U.S. 120, 139-140 (2017). "[T]he new-context inquiry is easily satisfied," encompassing cases with '"meaningful[ly]"' different facts, or "'potential special factors' "-including "alternative remedial structures"-" 'not consider[ed]"' in the Court's prior cases. Egbert v. Boule, 596 U.S. 482, 492-493 (2022). "[A] court may not recognize a Bivens remedy" if "there is any reason to think that Congress might be better equipped to create a damages remedy." Id . at 492. In this case, respondent alleged that he suffered a fractured coccyx in a prison gang fight, causing chronic pain, but was not sent to a hospital. The Ninth Circuit held the suit did not present a "new" context from Carlson -not-withstanding an alternative remedial scheme this Court did not consider in Carlson, and despite significant factual differences such as the immediacy and severity of the harm alleged. The question presented is: Whether the Ninth Circuit here erred in recognizing a Bivens cause of action.

lower_court_summary: Salazar subscribed to an online newsletter from 247Sports.com, a Paramount-owned site, and alleged that Paramount shared his video-viewing history with Facebook without his consent, in violation of the Video Privacy Protection Act. The Sixth Circuit held that the Act protects only people who rent, buy, or subscribe to audio-visual goods or services, so a newsletter subscriber is not a protected 'consumer.' It affirmed dismissal of his class action. Paramount won.
question_presented: The Video Privacy Protection Act (“VPPA”) contains a one-sentence liability clause. It prohibits a “video tape service provider” from “knowingly disclos[ing], to any person, personally identifiable information concerning any consumer of such provider.” 18 U.S.C. § 2710 (b)( 1 ). The statute defines “consumer” broadly to include a “subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider.” Id. § 2710 (a)( 1 ). It defines “personally identifiable information” to include information that “identifies a person as having requested or obtained specific video materials or services from a video tape service provider.” Id. § 2710 (a)( 3 ). And it defines “video tape service provider” to include those in the business of delivering audiovisual materials. Id . § 2710 (a)( 4 ). Paramount is a “video tape service provider.” Both courts below assumed as much. Michael Salazar subscribed to Paramount’s online newsletter, which he used to view videos. Paramount then disclosed Mr. Salazar’s Facebook ID and his video-watching history to Facebook. That information counts as “personally identifiable information.” Again, both courts below assumed as much. The question here is whether the phrase “goods or services from a video tape service provider,” as used in the VPPA’s definition of “consumer,” refers to all of a video tape service provider’s goods or services or only to its audiovisual goods or services.

case_name: Anderson v. Intel Corp. Investment Policy Committee
lower_court_summary: Participants in Intel's retirement plans sued the plans' managers under ERISA, alleging they acted imprudently by putting large amounts into hedge funds and private equity, and disloyally by favoring companies linked to Intel's venture-capital arm. The Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal. It held that a plaintiff who claims imprudence based on poor results must offer a meaningful comparison showing similar funds did better, which Anderson did not, and that he alleged no real conflict of interest. Intel's plan managers won.
question_presented: Under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA), a plan fiduciary is subject to a "[p]rudent man standard of care," which requires the fiduciary to "discharge his duties with respect to a plan" with the "care, skill, prudence, and diligence" that a prudent person "acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters would use." 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a) (1)). As this Court has recognized, a court's inquiry into whether a plaintiff has adequately alleged that a fiduciary breached ERISA's duty of prudence "will necessarily be context specific" because the content of that duty "turns on 'the circumstances ... prevailing' at the time the fiduciary acts." Fifth Third Bancorp. v. Dudenhoeffer, 573 U.S. 409, 425 (2014) (quoting 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B)). As a result, "categorical" pleading rules are "inconsistent with the context-specific inquiry that ERISA requires." Hughes v. Nw. Univ ., 595 U.S.170, 173 (2022). The question presented is: Whether, for claims predicated on fund underperformance, pleading that an ERISA fiduciary failed to use the requisite "care, skill, prudence, or diligence" under the circumstances and thus breached ERISA's duty of prudence when investing plan assets requires alleging a "meaningful benchmark."

case_name: Department of the Air Force v. Prutehi Guahan
lower_court_summary: A Guam environmental group challenged the Air Force's plan to burn and detonate old munitions at Tarague Beach, arguing the Air Force first had to do an environmental review under NEPA. The district court dismissed. A divided Ninth Circuit reversed, holding the group had standing, that the Air Force's application to renew its hazardous-waste (RCRA) permit was a final agency action courts can review, and that the RCRA permit process does not replace NEPA review. The environmental group won.
question_presented: The Resource Conservation and Recovery Act of 1976 (RCRA), 42 U.S.C. 6901 et seq ., is a comprehensive environmental statute providing for cradle-to-grave regulation of hazardous waste through a scheme of cooperative federalism. Under RCRA, the United States Environmental Protection Agency may authorize state and territorial regulators to administer permitting programs for hazardous-waste-treatment facilities in their respective jurisdictions, including facilities operated by the federal government. The questions presented are as follows: 1. Whether the federal government's submission to a state or territorial regulator of an application to renew a RCRA permit is "final agency action" that is immediately reviewable under the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. 704. 2. Whether the federal government must comply with the general environmental- review procedures of the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969, 42 U.S.C. 4321 et seq ., before submitting a permit-renewal application under RCRA, which sets forth its own specific procedures to review environmental impacts in the context of hazardous-waste treatment.

case_name: St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy
lower_court_summary: Colorado's universal preschool program requires participating preschools to agree not to turn away families on grounds including religion, sexual orientation and gender identity. Catholic parishes, the Archdiocese of Denver and parents argued this violates the First Amendment because Catholic preschools admit only families who support Catholic teaching. After a trial, the district court denied relief. The Tenth Circuit affirmed, holding the requirement is neutral and generally applicable and does not violate the First Amendment. Colorado won.
question_presented: 1. Whether proving a lack of general applicability under Employment Division v. Smith requires showing unfettered discretion or categorical exemptions for identical secular conduct. 2. Whether Carson v. Makin displaces the rule of Employment Division v. Smith only when the government explicitly excludes religious people and institutions.

lower_court_summary: Johnson, a veteran serving a state prison sentence, sued Congress after his disability benefits were cut under a law that limits payments to imprisoned veterans, arguing the law is unconstitutional. The Eleventh Circuit held that sovereign immunity bars suing Congress, and that renaming the defendant would not help because the Veterans' Judicial Review Act sends such challenges through a separate review system rather than district courts. It ordered the case dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. The government won.
question_presented: Did the Veterans' Judicial Review Act strip district courts of the jurisdiction, recognized by this Court in Johnson v. Robison, 415 U.S. 361 (1974), to hear challenges to the constitutionality of acts of Congress affecting veterans' benefits?

case_name: International Partners for Ethical Care, Inc. v. Ferguson
lower_court_summary: A parents' organization and parents of children with gender dysphoria challenged Washington laws that let minors get shelter services and some mental-health care without their parents being told, arguing the laws violate parental rights. The Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding the plaintiffs lacked standing because they showed neither a current injury nor a sufficiently likely future one, such as their child running away. Washington State won.
question_presented: The "interest of parents in the care, custody, and control of their children" is perhaps the oldest of the fundamental liberty interests recognized by this Court." Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57, 65 (2000). But that right is mere rhetoric if federal judges bar parents from court via a miserly interpretation of standing doctrine-a question, as three Justices recently recognized, that is of "great and growing national importance." Lee v. Poudre Sch. Dist. R-1, 607 U.S. --, 2025 WL 2906469, *1 (2025) (Alita, J., statement) (citation omitted). It is certainly important to Petitioners, who are parents of gender-confused children (including one child who previously ran away) and who do not wish to affirm that confusion. They challenged Washington laws designed to give runaway minors "gender affirming treatment" without parental notice or consent. But despite their being the challenged laws' target, and despite their alleging specific current harms and a substantial risk of specific future harms to their ability to parent, the Ninth Circuit held that Petitioners lacked Article III standing. The question presented is: Whether parents have standing to challenge a law or policy that deliberately displaces their decision-making role as to "gender transitions" of their children, and in so doing creates present and likely future impediments to their ability to parent their children as they deem best for them.

lower_court_summary: Wassily and another noncitizen had been granted asylum, but their asylum was later terminated. They sought permanent residence under a law that allows adjustment for any noncitizen 'granted asylum.' The Second Circuit held that the law covers only people who currently hold asylum status, not people whose asylum was terminated, and denied their petitions for review. One judge dissented. The government won.
question_presented: The asylum laws offer protection against removal for certain noncitizens in this country who suffered past persecution or reasonably fear future persecution in their country of nationality. For those “granted asylum,” the immigration laws also provide a pathway to obtain lawful permanent resident (LPR) status. Under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b), the government "may adjust to the status of an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence the status of any alien granted asylum," if certain statutory criteria are satisfied. The question presented is: Whether noncitizens who were "granted asylum," but whose asylum was later terminated, are eligible for adjustment to LPR status under Section 1159(b) (as the Fifth Circuit held), or are categorically ineligible (as the Second and Fourth Circuits held)?

case_name: Grand v. City of University Heights
lower_court_summary: Grand, an Orthodox Jewish resident of University Heights, Ohio, hosted group prayer at his home, and the city told him he needed a special-use permit to use his home as a place of religious assembly. He applied, withdrew the application before the city made a final decision, and then sued the city and its officials under federal civil-rights and religious-liberty laws. The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the city, holding that some claims were not ripe because the city never made a final decision and that the rest failed on the merits. The city won.
question_presented: Whether the First Amendment's established chilling-effect doctrine-under which a credible government threat that deters the exercise of fundamental rights constitutes a complete and independently actionable constitutional injury-is displaced by Williamson Cnty .'s land-use finality requirement when a plaintiff alleges that government threats both before and after a Planning Commission meeting chilled religious exercise, worship, and assembly.

case_name: Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC
lower_court_summary: The Department of Labor ordered Sun Valley Orchards, a New Jersey farm, to pay civil penalties and back wages in the agency's own in-house proceedings for allegedly breaking H-2A guest-worker program rules. The farm sued, and the district court dismissed. The Third Circuit reversed, holding, under the Supreme Court's decision in SEC v. Jarkesy, that the farm was entitled to have the case decided by a federal court rather than by the agency. The farm won.
question_presented: 1) Whether Article III of the Constitution precludes the Department of Labor from adjudicating proceedings to collect monetary remedies from employers who have allegedly violated the terms and conditions of employment of H-2A workers and domestic workers in corresponding employment. 2) Whether 8 U.S.C. §1188(g)(2) authorizes the Department of Labor to adjudicate proceedings to collect monetary remedies from employers who have allegedly violated the terms and conditions of employment of H-2A workers and domestic workers in corresponding employment.

lower_court_summary: Dexter Johnson, sentenced to death in Texas for a 2006 murder, sought to bring a second federal habeas petition claiming he is intellectually disabled and so cannot be executed under Atkins v. Virginia. Federal law sharply limits second petitions. The district court ruled the claim could go forward because it had effectively been unavailable to him earlier. In an unpublished opinion, the Fifth Circuit affirmed. The prisoner won.
question_presented: The Anti-Terrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA) prohibits successive habeas applications by state prisoners with only narrow exceptions, including for claims that "rel[y] on a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable." 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(A). Near-identical language allows federal prisoners to file a successive habeas motion that contains "a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable." Id. § 2255(h)(2). The courts of appeals are divided over whether claims rely on "a new rule ... that was previously unavailable" when a claim based on the rule could have been raised in an earlier federal habeas petition but would not have succeeded. The Eleventh and Fourth Circuits hold that whether a claim would have been meritorious does not affect whether the rule was previously available. In the decision below, the Fifth Circuit adhered to its view (and that of the Ninth Circuit) that a claim was previously available only if it had "some possibility of merit" based on the evidence available to the petitioner at the time of an earlier petition. The question presented is: Whether a claim relies on a "a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable" when the habeas petitioner could have asserted a claim based on the rule in a prior federal habeas petition.

case_name: Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota
lower_court_summary: Civil-rights groups, Native American tribes, the Democratic Party and the United States challenged 2022 Arizona laws that require documentary proof of citizenship and other information to register and vote, and that direct officials to check voters' citizenship. A divided Ninth Circuit largely affirmed the district court: it held many provisions conflict with the National Voter Registration Act, an earlier consent decree, or the Civil Rights Act, rejected an equal-protection claim, and sent one finding about legislative intent back for reconsideration. The Republican National Committee and Arizona legislative leaders, who defended the laws, lost on most issues.
question_presented: Like every other State, Arizona permits only United States citizens to vote in federal elections. To enforce that qualification, Arizona requires every applicant who registers to vote to produce "satisfactory evidence of citizenship." Ariz. Rev. Stat. §16-121.01(C). If election officials obtain "information" from periodic inspections of Arizona's voter rolls that "confirms" a "person registered is not a United States citizen," they "cancel the registration." Id . §16-165(A) (10). The Ninth Circuit held that the National Voter Registration Act-52 U.S.C. §§20506(a)(6) (A)(ii), 20508(b)(1), 20507(c)(2)(a)-preempts those provisions of Arizona law. It also held that Arizona cannot require voter-registration applicants to produce proof of citizenship because in 2018, a previous Arizona Secretary of State entered a consent decree with private litigants. This Court has granted an emergency stay on each issue: One in this case and one in a Fourth Circuit case. The RNC raises both questions here on the merits. The questions presented are: (1) Does the National Voter Registration Act or a federal consent decree prohibit Arizona from requiring voter-registration applicants to produce "satisfactory evidence" of U.S. citizenship when registering with a state registration form? (2) Does the National Voter Registration Act prohibit Arizona from implementing a program within 90 days of a federal election to cancel the registrations of voters who are not U.S. citizens?

case_name: U.S. DOGE Service v. United States District Court for the District of Columbia
lower_court: U.S. Court of Appeals, D.C. Circuit
lower_court_summary: In a Freedom of Information Act suit, the watchdog group CREW sought records from the U.S. DOGE Service, and the district court allowed discovery into whether DOGE is an 'agency' covered by FOIA. The government asked the D.C. Circuit for a writ of mandamus to block the discovery. After the Supreme Court ordered the discovery narrowed, the D.C. Circuit granted mandamus only as to requests CREW had already withdrawn and otherwise let discovery proceed. CREW largely won.
question_presented: The district court in this case entered a wide-ranging and intrusive discovery order against the U.S. DOGE Service (USDS)-a body within the Executive Office of the President tasked with advising the President-to determine whether that body's influence renders it an "agency" subject to the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), 5 U.S.C. 552. This Court previously granted certiorari, vacated the court of appeals' denial of a writ of mandamus, and remanded for the court of appeals to "narrow" discovery in light of "separation of powers concerns." On remand, respondent withdrew several of its discovery requests, and the court of appeals again denied the government's mandamus petition without any new analysis regarding the remaining discovery, which includes numerous requests for internal communications and a deposition of USDS's head. The questions presented are: 1. Whether the court of appeals' order departed from this Court's instructions and the separation-of-powers principles that this Court articulated in Cheney v. United States District Court, 542 U.S. 367 (2004). 2. Whether a court may order broad discovery against an Executive Office advisory body-potentially providing much information sought on the merits of a plaintiffs FOIA claims-to determine whether FOIA's disclosure requirements apply in the first place.

case_name: Missionaries of St. John the Baptist, Inc. v. Frederic
lower_court_summary: A Catholic organization sought zoning approval to build an outdoor grotto shrine to the Virgin Mary next to its church in Park Hills, Kentucky, and neighbors challenged the approval in court. The Kentucky Supreme Court held that applying the city's zoning ordinance to stop the shrine did not violate the federal religious land-use law (RLUIPA), affirming the lower appeals court on different reasoning. The neighbors won; the religious organization lost.
question_presented: Whether a land-use regulation that prohibits a religious institution from building a religious structure on its own property constitutes a "substantial burden" on religious exercise under the Substantial Burden Provision of the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA), 42 U.S.C. § 2000cc(a).

lower_court_summary: Montoya Palacios won a habeas case challenging his immigration detention and then asked the government to pay his attorney fees under the Equal Access to Justice Act. The district court denied fees because Fourth Circuit precedent holds that a habeas case is not a 'civil action' covered by that Act. At his own request, the Fourth Circuit summarily affirmed so he could seek Supreme Court review. The government won.
question_presented: The Equal Access to Justice Act (EAJA) provides that, "in any civil action (other than cases sounding in tort)" by or against the federal government, a court shall award to a prevailing party its fees and costs, unless the court finds certain exceptions present. 28 U.S.C. § 2412(d) (1)(A). The question presented is whether, under EAJA, "any civil action" encompasses an action seeking a writ of habeas corpus to challenge civil immigration detention.

case_name: Apple Inc. v. Epic Games, Inc.
lower_court_summary: After Epic's antitrust suit, a court order barred Apple from stopping app developers from pointing customers to ways of paying outside the App Store. The district court found Apple in civil contempt for responding with a large commission on outside purchases and limits on how links could look. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the contempt finding and most of the remedy, reversed one part of the sanctions for further proceedings, and refused to dissolve the injunction or assign a new judge. Epic largely won.
question_presented: Whether a court may hold a party in civil contempt based on a violation of an injunction's "spirit" where the injunction is silent as to the conduct upon which contempt is based, as the Ninth Circuit holds; or, instead, whether a court must ground a finding of civil contempt on the violation of an order that clearly and unambiguously proscribes the precise conduct at issue, as other circuits hold.

lower_court_summary: Ozurumba, a Nigerian citizen, was denied asylum and protection from removal because an immigration judge found he gave 'material support' to a terrorist group when he was forced to cook meals for its leaders. A divided Fourth Circuit granted his petition for review, holding the record did not support a finding of material support under the statute, and sent the case back to the Board of Immigration Appeals. Ozurumba won.
question_presented: An alien is removable and ineligible for various immigration benefits if he has provided material support to a terrorist organization. The question presented is whether, under 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(3)(B)(iv)(Vl), such support must advance the organization's actual commission of terrorism to qualify for that bar.

lower_court_summary: In a divorce settlement, Roxane Marschner was to receive part of her ex-husband's military retirement pay. He later gave up that pay in exchange for disability pay, which federal law does not let states divide, and the trial court ordered him to make up her loss under an indemnification clause. The North Dakota Supreme Court reversed, holding that federal law bars state courts from dividing military disability pay, including by enforcing such a clause. The ex-husband won.
question_presented: In the Uniformed Services Former Spouses' Protection Act ("USFSPA"), Congress provided that a State may treat veterans' longevity-based retirement pay as divisible property in divorce. 10 U.S.C. § 1408(c). But Congress further provided that retirement pay that was waived to receive disability pay, as well as certain retirement pay received due to disability-related retirements, would be indivisible. 10 U.S.C. § 408(a)(4)(A)(ii), (iii). In Howell v. Howell, 581 U.S. 214 (2017), a divorced veteran waived a portion of his longevity-based retirement pay in order to receive disability pay, causing his ex- wife's share of his retirement pay to decrease. The divorce court ordered him to indemnify his ex-wife for that reduction. This Court held that the USFSPA preempted that indemnification order. See id . at 222. In this case, unlike in Howell, the parties agreed as part of their divorce settlement that the veteran would indemnify his ex-wife if her share of his retirement pay were reduced because he later waived his retirement pay to receive disability benefits or because he received disability-based retirement pay. Even though the veteran agreed to the indemnification provision at the time of the divorce, the North Dakota Supreme Court nonetheless held that, under Howell, enforcement of the indemnification provision was preempted. The question presented is: Does the USFSPA require state courts to refuse enforcement of indemnification provisions in divorce settlement agreements?

lower_court_summary: Beaird pleaded guilty to possessing a firearm as a convicted felon and was sentenced to 72 months. His sentence was increased under a guideline that, according to the Sentencing Guidelines' official commentary, treats his 17-round magazine as a 'large capacity magazine.' In an unpublished opinion, the Fifth Circuit affirmed, holding all his challenges, including to the court's reliance on that commentary, foreclosed by its own precedent. The United States won.
question_presented: Whether Stinson v. United States, 508 U.S. 36 (1993), still correctly states the rule for the deference that courts must give the commentary to the sentencing guidelines.

lower_court_summary: Maxwell, a federal prisoner, filed a habeas petition seeking transfer to a halfway house or home confinement based on time credits under the First Step Act. The district court dismissed it for failure to use the prison's internal complaint process first. The Fifth Circuit affirmed on a different ground: under its rule, claims that would not automatically lead to earlier release must be brought as civil-rights suits, not habeas petitions. The prison warden won.
question_presented: Whether a claim regarding application of time credits under the First Step Act of 2018, 132 Stat. 5195–5208 (codified in relevant part at 18 U.S.C. §§ 3631–3635), seeking accelerated transfer to a halfway house or home confinement, can be brought in a habeas petition under 28 U.S.C. § 2241.

lower_court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, 4th District
lower_court_summary: Kian was convicted by a six-person jury in Florida of the felony of practicing chiropractic medicine with a suspended license, and was sentenced to prison followed by probation. Florida's intermediate appeals court affirmed in a one-word decision without an opinion. The State won.
question_presented: Whether Petitioner was deprived of his right, under the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments, to a trial by a 12-person jury when the defendant is charged with a serious felony? There are two other petitions raising the same question presented. See Parada v. United States, No. 25-166; Minor v. Florida, No. 24-7489. This case should at least be held pending resolution of those petitions.

lower_court_summary: Berry, a federal prisoner, challenged his conviction for brandishing a firearm during an attempted carjacking, arguing it may have rested on a part of the statute the Supreme Court later struck down (United States v. Davis). The district court denied relief. The Eleventh Circuit refused a certificate of appealability, holding that binding circuit precedent requires him to show his conviction more likely than not rested on the invalid part, so reasonable jurists could not debate the result. The United States won.
question_presented: Under the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA), an appeal may not be taken from a final order in a federal habeas proceeding unless a circuit judge or justice issues a "certificate of appealability" (COA). 28 U.S.C.§ 2253(c (1). A COA may issue only if the prisoner makes a "substantial showing of the denial of a constitutional right." 28 U.S.C. § 2253(c)(2). To do so, the prisoner must show that "reasonable jurists could debate" whether the petition should have been resolved in a different manner. Slack v. McDaniel, 529 U.S. 473, A484 (2000). The question presented is: Whether a certificate of appealability under 28 U.S.C. § 2253 should be granted where the issue that the petitioner seeks to raise on appeal has been resolved against him by binding circuit precedent but has been resolved in his favor by another circuit.

lower_court_summary: Barbosa da Cunha, a Brazilian citizen who entered the U.S. without inspection around 2005 and had applied for asylum, was arrested in 2025 and held without bond under the government's view that the law requires detention. The district court granted his habeas petition and ordered a bond hearing, after which he was released on bond. The Second Circuit affirmed, holding that noncitizens who entered without inspection and were not caught at the border fall under the provision that allows bond, not the mandatory-detention provision. The noncitizen won.
question_presented: Whether 8 U.S.C. 1225(b)(2)(A) mandates the detention pending removal proceedings of aliens who, like respondent, are present in the United States without having been admitted.

case_name: Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education
lower_court_summary: A parent group claimed that Montgomery County, Maryland's new admissions policy for magnet middle schools discriminated against Asian American students, in violation of equal protection. The district court dismissed, finding the complaint did not plausibly allege that the policy hurt Asian American students as a group or that it was adopted with discriminatory intent. In an unpublished opinion, the Fourth Circuit affirmed, applying its earlier Coalition for TJ decision, which the group admitted bound the panel. The school board won.
question_presented: Whether a plaintiff challenging a facially neutral admissions policy as racially discriminatory must establish that the targeted racial group suffered an aggregate disparate impact relative to its share of the applicant pool.

lower_court_summary: Home-distilling hobbyists and their association challenged a federal law, dating from 1868, that bans distilling spirits at home. The district court ruled for them. The Fifth Circuit affirmed in large part, holding that the ban exceeds Congress's taxing power and the Necessary and Proper Clause because it reduces rather than protects tax revenue, and it reversed a partial dismissal so more plaintiffs could proceed. The home distillers won.
question_presented: Since the Founding era, Congress has imposed an excise tax on the production of distilled spirits. After documenting the extensive evasion of the government's efforts to collect the tax, Congress enacted a comprehensive scheme requiring distillation stills to be licensed and subject to inspection. One aspect of the scheme prohibited stills from being located in various places, including within residential properties-a restriction that has now been in effect for 160 years. In the decision below, the Fifth Circuit held that the location restrictions exceed Congress's enumerated powers, in direct conflict with a decision of the Sixth Circuit upholding the restriction on home distilling. The question presented is as follows: Whether the prohibition on the production of distilled spirits in particular locations, including "in any dwelling house" or "in any shed, yard, or inclosure connected with any dwelling house," 26 U.S.C. 5178(a)(1)(B), is necessary and proper for carrying into execution Congress's enumerated power to lay and collect taxes.

case_name: Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D.
lower_court_summary: A class of noncitizens with final removal orders challenged Department of Homeland Security guidance that allows deportation to 'third countries' (not their home country) without notice and a chance to raise a fear of persecution or torture there. The district court declared the policy unlawful, set it aside, and declared class members entitled to notice and a chance to object. The First Circuit largely affirmed, holding the court had jurisdiction, classwide relief was allowed, and federal law requires such notice and a chance to object, though it found the plaintiffs lacked standing on one issue about the order of countries. The noncitizen class won.
question_presented: (1) Whether the district court had jurisdiction over Respondents’ claims. (2) Whether the district court had authority to enter classwide declaratory relief and APA vacatur under 8 U.S.C. §1252(f)(1). (3) Whether the Government’s Guidance on third-country removals is unlawful under 8 U.S.C. §1231(b), the Due Process Clause, or FARRA/CAT and its implementing regulations. (4) Such other questions that the Government determines are appropriate for the proper disposition of the case.

lower_court_summary: Two lawful permanent residents were held for months under the mandatory-detention immigration law without bond hearings. The Second Circuit held that due process forbids unreasonably prolonged detention under that law without a bond hearing, and ruled for both detainees. The case was dismissed by agreement of the parties (Rule 46) on September 11, 2026, before argument. Not rated.
question_presented: 1. Whether there is a point at which an alien's detention under Section 1226(c), pending a decision on whether he is to be removed, becomes "unreasonably prolonged," such that due process requires a bond hearing. 2. If so, whether, in such a bond hearing, due process requires placing the burden on the government to justify the alien's continued detention by clear and convincing evidence. [Added by the Court:] Whether G.M.'s case is now moot.
